The maternal investment in producing such well-developed pups is considerable, as each female produces only a limited number of offspring per reproductive cycle. These neonates are immediately capable of benthic foraging, preying upon small crustaceans and polychaetes. The relatively advanced state of development at birth likely reduces early-life mortality compared to species that hatch at a smaller size, providing a demographic advantage in the cool, productive waters surrounding New Zealand. This life-history strategy of producing few but large offspring is typical of many elasmobranchs.

Females of this species attain a considerably larger body size than males, with the maximum recorded pelvic length reaching 91.3 centimeters [Li = 91.3 centimeters]. Reproductive output in Zearaja nasuta is characterized by a notably low maximum rate. Under the cool, stable conditions found at depths typical of this species, the maximum annual reproductive rate is approximately 2 pups per year [Ri = approximately 2 pups per year]. This slow replacement rate places considerable demographic pressure on populations, rendering them highly vulnerable to overfishing. The current stock status of the New Zealand rough skate is considered to be depleted in some regions, a direct consequence of its low intrinsic rate of increase coupled with decades of bycatch in trawl fisheries.
